title: The bronze (raw) layer
summary: Landing source data append-only and replayable, with the metadata, retention and privacy rules that make it trustworthy.

blocks.text: Bronze is the system of record for **what the sources sent and when**. Its job is narrow: capture every delivery completely, never lose or silently alter data, and make it possible to rebuild everything downstream. Business logic does not belong here. A good bronze layer is boring, and boring is the point.
13.1 Principles of the raw layer

items: **Append-only**: new deliveries are added, existing rows are never updated in place. Corrections from the source arrive as new records.
**Faithful**: keep source values as delivered, including bad dates and odd encodings. Parse failures are recorded, not dropped.
**Complete metadata**: every row says where it came from and when it arrived.
**Source-aligned**: one bronze table per source entity or feed, named after the source (`bronze.crm__contacts`), not after business concepts.
**Replayable**: silver can be rebuilt from bronze alone, for any date range.

blocks.text: Some teams keep the original files (JSON, CSV, Avro) in object storage as a *landing* zone and load bronze tables from them; others write bronze tables directly from connectors. Either works if one of the two is the durable, immutable copy and the retention policy says which.
13.2 Metadata columns

Metadata columns are cheap to add at ingestion and impossible to reconstruct later. Standardise them across all bronze tables so tooling (deduplication macros, freshness checks, lineage) works everywhere.

head: Column
Meaning
Why it matters
rows: When the platform received the record
System and table, topic or endpoint
Object path and row within it
Trace any row back to the exact delivered file
Exactly-once reasoning, ordering within a partition, replay from offset
CDC operation: c (create), u (update), d (delete), r (snapshot read)
Commit time and log position in the source database
Ordering changes to the same key

blocks.title: Loading files into bronze with metadata (Snowflake)
blocks.text:
COPY INTO bronze.shop__orders (raw, _source_file, _file_row_number, _ingested_at)
FROM (
  SELECT $1,
         METADATA$FILENAME,
         METADATA$FILE_ROW_NUMBER,
         CURRENT_TIMESTAMP()
  FROM @landing/shop/orders/
)
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = 'JSON')
ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE';

`ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE'` keeps loading past bad rows, which is right for bronze only if rejected rows are counted and alerted on: the load history (for example `COPY_HISTORY`) reports error counts and first errors per file. Some validation features do not support COPY statements with transformations, so check the documentation for your load pattern. Silent loss is the one thing bronze must never do.
13.3 Schema-on-read and schema evolution

Bronze is usually **schema-on-read**: payloads are stored as a semi-structured column (`VARIANT` in Snowflake, a string or `variant` type in Spark/Delta, or the raw file) or with a permissive inferred schema. Types and meaning are applied in silver. This means a new field in the source never breaks ingestion, and a removed field shows up as NULLs rather than a failed load.

head: Approach
Pros
Cons
rows: Whole payload in one semi-structured column
Never breaks on schema change; exact copy
Every consumer must parse; weaker pruning
Inferred typed columns with schema evolution
Type changes (int to string) can still fail or coerce silently
Typed columns plus a `_rescued_data` or overflow column
Typed for known fields, nothing lost for unknown ones
Two places to look for a field

blocks.text: Schema-on-read does not mean no schema awareness. Monitor bronze for new, missing and type-changed fields and alert the owning team: schema drift caught in bronze is a ticket; caught in a CFO dashboard it is an incident.
13.4 Landing CDC streams

Change data capture (chapter 17) produces a stream of row-level events. Land them as **events, not state**: one bronze row per change, with the operation, the before and/or after image and the ordering columns. Do not apply the changes in bronze.

blocks.title: A Debezium-style update event (simplified)
blocks.text:
{
  "before": {"id": 42, "status": "pending", "amount": 120.00},
  "after":  {"id": 42, "status": "paid",    "amount": 120.00},
  "source": {"db": "shop", "table": "orders", "lsn": 98123456, "ts_ms": 1763380000000},
  "op": "u",
  "ts_ms": 1763380000412
}

items: Keep `before`, `after`, `op` and the source position. Deletes carry only `before` (and may be followed by a tombstone record with a null value in Kafka, used for log compaction).
Flattening `after` into columns in bronze is acceptable if the full envelope is also kept or the original stream is retained.
Initial snapshots (`op = r`) and ongoing changes land in the same table so silver can rebuild state from either.

blocks.text: 13.5 Replayability, idempotency and retention

Replay means two things: rebuilding silver from bronze, and re-ingesting into bronze without creating duplicates. The second requires idempotent loads. Typical techniques: file-level load tracking (Snowflake `COPY INTO` skips files it has already loaded, for a limited history window; Spark Auto Loader and similar tools keep checkpoints), delete-and-reload by `_batch_id`, or offset-tracked streaming writes.
Bronze grows forever unless you decide otherwise. Volume is usually the largest in the platform because it keeps every change event and every daily full extract. Set retention per source:

items: **CDC event streams**: keep long enough to rebuild silver state, or keep a compacted snapshot plus recent events.
**Daily full extracts**: older days often add nothing beyond what silver SCD history holds; keep weeks to months, then compact.
**Regulated data**: retention set by legal requirements, which may require keeping years or deleting within days.
Use cold storage tiers for old landing files; object storage at a few cents per GB-month makes raw history cheap, but compute to scan it is not.

blocks.text: 13.6 PII and secrets in raw data

Bronze inevitably contains the most sensitive data in the platform: unmasked emails, addresses, sometimes free text with health or payment details, and occasionally credentials accidentally logged by the source. Treat it accordingly.

items: Restrict access to bronze to the ingestion and platform roles; analysts read silver and gold.
Classify columns on arrival (tags or catalog classification) so masking policies follow the data downstream (chapter 34).
For fields that must never be stored in clear (card numbers, national IDs), tokenise or hash them **before** landing, in the ingestion path.

Plan for erasure requests: an append-only, immutable bronze makes GDPR deletion hard. Options include crypto-shredding (encrypt per-subject data with a key you can destroy) or row-level deletes with table formats that support them followed by snapshot expiry (chapter 25).

blocks.text: Deleting a row from an Iceberg or Delta table does not remove it from storage until old snapshots are expired and unreferenced files are cleaned up. Time travel is, by definition, a copy of the data you deleted. Erasure processes must include snapshot expiry.

blocks.title: Rebuilding after a silver bug
blocks.text: A pricing team discovered that silver had applied the wrong currency conversion for six weeks. Because bronze held every order event with `_source_ts` and `_ingested_at`, the data team fixed the silver model and backfilled exactly those six weeks, partition by partition, then rebuilt affected gold aggregates.
items: No re-extraction from the source, which only kept 30 days of history
The backfill was reproducible and reviewed as a normal pull request
Finance received corrected numbers with a full audit trail

blocks.title: Design bronze for three feeds
blocks.text: You ingest (a) a Postgres orders database via CDC into Kafka, (b) a nightly CSV export of 20 million product records from a supplier SFTP, and (c) a SaaS marketing API returning JSON pages. For each, define the bronze table shape, metadata columns, idempotency mechanism and retention, and how you would handle a customer's erasure request.
hints: Which feed can be re-requested from the source and for how long?
Is a nightly full extract of 20 million rows worth keeping forever?

items: Bronze is append-only, faithful and source-aligned; business logic waits for silver.
Standard metadata columns (ingestion time, source file, offsets, op type, batch id) are cheap now and impossible later.
Schema-on-read keeps ingestion robust, but schema drift must still be monitored.
Land CDC as events with ordering columns; apply them in silver.
Plan retention, access control and erasure for the most sensitive layer in the platform.

blocks.q: A source adds a new JSON field. Bronze stores the payload in a VARIANT column. What happens?
options: The field lands with the payload; silver decides when to extract it
The load fails until the table is altered
blocks.explain: Schema-on-read stores whatever arrives. Ingestion keeps working, and silver adopts the new field deliberately. Drift monitoring should still flag it.

blocks.q: Which metadata column lets you trace a bronze row to the exact object it came from?
blocks.explain: File path and row number identify the exact delivered record. Ingestion time is shared by many files loaded together.

blocks.q: Why should CDC changes not be applied as updates in bronze?
options: MERGE is not supported on object storage
Keeping events preserves history and replayability; state is derived in silver
blocks.explain: Applying changes in bronze discards the change history and makes bronze no longer a faithful record. Table formats do support MERGE; that is not the reason.

blocks.q: After deleting a person's rows from an Iceberg bronze table, what else is required for erasure?
options: Nothing, deletes are immediate on storage
Expire old snapshots and remove unreferenced files
blocks.explain: Old snapshots still reference files containing the data, and time travel can read them. Snapshot expiry and orphan-file cleanup physically remove it.
